sections.title: The Leap from Concrete to Abstract
sections.content: Briefly review 2D/3D vectors (arrows in space). Introduce the core idea: a vector space isn't just about arrows; it's about a 'system' of objects that follow a specific set of rules (axioms).
sections.example: Visual transition: A 2D coordinate grid morphing into a collection of abstract 'data points' and 'functions'.

sections.title: The Rules of the Game: Defining Vector Spaces
sections.content: Introduce the two fundamental operations: Vector Addition and Scalar Multiplication. Explain that any set can be a 'Vector Space' if it satisfies the 8 axioms (Closure, Commutativity, Associativity, Identity, Inverse, etc.).
sections.example: Animation: A 'Robot Chef' mixing ingredients. If adding two ingredients (vectors) results in something that is still a valid dish (closure) and follows specific rules, the kitchen is a vector space.

sections.title: Case Study: Beyond Geometric Arrows
sections.content: Demonstrate that polynomials or continuous functions are also vectors. Show how the 'zero vector' becomes the 'zero polynomial' (f(x)=0).
sections.example: Visual comparison: An arrow (v) next to a polynomial (P(x) = ax^2 + bx + c). Both share the same algebraic structure, even if they look different.

sections.title: Visualizing Abstract Dimensions
sections.content: Explain that dimension in an abstract space relates to the number of basis elements needed to represent any object in that space.
sections.example: Animation: A pixelated character. We can describe the character as a sum of base images (basis vectors). Changing the coefficients changes the character's appearance, illustrating linear combinations.

sections.title: Summary and Real-World Application
sections.content: Conclude with the importance of abstraction: It allows us to apply the same geometric intuition (like projection and distance) to complex datasets like audio signals or neural network weights.
sections.example: A final visual: A digital 'Signal Wave' and a '3D Coordinate Arrow' side-by-side, both being processed by the same mathematical 'Toolbox'.
